Describes a correct target-setting methodology
Correctly addresses scale-out lag
Gives a reasonable minReplicas consideration

questions.title: Designing a Shared Feature Store and Training-Checkpoint Strategy for a Mid-Size ML Platform Team
questions.prompt: You're the platform engineer for a company with roughly 30 production models across 4 teams, currently each building its own ad hoc feature pipelines and saving checkpoints with plain torch.save on local disk. Design a shared feature store and a training-checkpoint strategy that this platform team can actually operate and that the model teams will actually adopt. Walk through requirements, the core design, how data flows through it, and the real failure modes and tradeoffs you'd accept.
commonMistakes: Designing for sub-second feature freshness everywhere when most needs are minutes-to-hours
Choosing a checkpoint format coupled to current, small scale instead of one that survives future growth
Ignoring adoption and incentive risk; a platform nobody actually uses isn't solving the problem
Building custom tooling for commodity problems instead of adopting proven open-source components
No retention policy, leading to unbounded storage cost growth
keyPoints: Batch materialization as the default, streaming reserved for genuinely freshness-sensitive features
Point-in-time joins are non-negotiable to prevent training/serving skew and leakage
DCP, not plain torch.save, from day one so checkpointing survives a future move to multi-GPU training
Checkpoints and features alike need object storage with an explicit retention policy, not local disk or unbounded growth
Adoption risk, teams bypassing the platform, is as real a failure mode as a technical one

deepDive.heading: Clarify Requirements and Constraints
deepDive.content: Before designing anything, I'd pin down what the 4 teams actually need versus what sounds impressive to build. Freshness: most features for a 30-model org are almost certainly minutes-to-hours fresh, not sub-second, so I'd confirm that rather than assume every team needs streaming. Scale trajectory: are these training jobs single-GPU today with some teams likely to grow into multi-GPU FSDP jobs, which changes what checkpoint format is actually safe to standardize on now. Operability: a platform team supporting 30 models across 4 teams cannot realistically run something that needs a dedicated SRE rotation; whatever I design has to be operable by the platform team's actual staffing. And adoption friction: if migrating a feature or a checkpoint path costs a team a week of work with no visible payoff, they won't do it voluntarily, so the design has to make the easy path the right path.

deepDive.heading: Core Design: The Feature Store
deepDive.content: Offline store sits on the existing warehouse or data lake, no new storage system introduced. Online store is a managed key-value store, Redis or DynamoDB-class, sized for single-digit-millisecond reads. FeatureView definitions are versioned in git, giving every team the same discoverability and review process they already use for code. Batch materialization is the default pattern for essentially every feature, since most freshness needs are minutes to hours; streaming ingestion is reserved for the rare feature that genuinely needs sub-minute freshness, kept as an opt-in exception rather than the default architecture. Every training set is built through the framework's point-in-time historical-features API, never a raw join against the feature table's current state, specifically to prevent future information from leaking into historical training rows.

deepDive.heading: Core Design: The Checkpoint Strategy
deepDive.content: torch.distributed.checkpoint, DCP, is the standard for any job using more than one GPU, regardless of today's scale, because a model that starts single-GPU and grows into FSDP shouldn't need a checkpoint-format migration later just because nobody planned for growth up front. Checkpoints are written to object storage, never local disk, with an explicit retention policy: keep the last N checkpoints plus periodic milestone snapshots, rather than unbounded accumulation. A reproducibility bundle, pinned dependencies, the git commit SHA, the data version, and the full training config, is logged alongside every checkpoint through the existing experiment tracker, so a checkpoint is never just weights with no record of how they were produced.

deepDive.heading: Data and Control Flow
deepDive.content: A feature gets registered once in the git-versioned FeatureView. A scheduled materialization job copies values from the offline store into the online store on a cadence matched to that feature's actual freshness need. A training job reads historical features through the point-in-time API, builds its training set, trains with DCP checkpointing to object storage, and logs its reproducibility bundle. The exact same FeatureView definition serves the model online at inference time through the key-value store, with no separate reimplementation of the feature logic. Promotion, moving a trained model to production, happens by reassigning a registry alias, which the serving layer resolves at load time, so nothing about this flow requires a redeploy for a routine model update.

deepDive.heading: Failure Modes and Tradeoffs
deepDive.content: The most likely technical failure mode isn't a crash, it's training/serving skew creeping back in if a team bypasses the feature store for a 'quick' ad hoc feature under deadline pressure, which is an adoption risk as much as a technical one. Online store latency can become the new serving bottleneck if it's undersized for read volume, so capacity planning for the online store itself matters, not just the offline pipeline. Checkpoint storage cost will grow unbounded without the retention policy actually being enforced, not just documented. And the deliberate tradeoff I'd accept up front is a freshness ceiling from batch-only materialization as the default -- genuinely accepting that some features will be minutes stale, in exchange for a system the platform team can actually operate, with streaming added only where a real feature genuinely needs it, not preemptively everywhere.

deepDive.heading: What I'd Explicitly Not Build Yet
deepDive.content: No custom feature-serving SDK, no bespoke checkpoint format, and no streaming-everywhere architecture, since none of those are this company's differentiator and all three are commodity problems with proven open-source solutions already available, a Feast-style feature store and PyTorch's own DCP. Building them in-house would cost real engineering time to produce something worse than what already exists, and would saddle a 4-person-equivalent platform team with maintenance burden on infrastructure that isn't where the company's actual advantage lives.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly scopes requirements before designing, freshness needs, scale trajectory, operability
Feature store design is architecturally sound: offline/online split, point-in-time joins, batch-default
Checkpoint strategy correctly anticipates future multi-GPU scale via DCP and addresses storage/retention
Identifies real failure modes including adoption risk, not just technical risk
Shows build-vs-buy judgment, avoiding unnecessary custom tooling

questions.title: Designing Gang Scheduling and Queue Weights for a Shared Multi-Team Training Cluster
questions.prompt: Two teams, language-modeling and multimodal, submit large, multi-node distributed training jobs to one shared GPU cluster using Volcano. Design the queueing policy so the higher-priority team gets a larger share of capacity during contention, without letting the lower-priority team starve, and without letting two large jobs deadlock each other.
questions.modelAnswer: Each team gets its own Volcano Queue with a weight reflecting its relative priority, for example language-modeling weight 2 and multimodal weight 1, controlling the proportional share each gets when both want capacity at once, plus a separate capability cap on each queue so no single team can claim the entire cluster even during a period when the other team has no jobs running, protecting the lower-priority team from true starvation. Every large job is submitted as a gang-scheduled PodGroup with minMember set to its full required pod count, so Volcano holds all of a job's pods Pending until there's enough simultaneous capacity for the whole group, preventing the deadlock case where two large jobs each partially schedule and each end up holding GPUs the other needs to complete its own group. If total cluster capacity falls short even for the highest-priority queue's job, that's a signal for the autoscaler to provision additional nodes rather than the scheduler trying to force a fit that isn't there.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd give each team its own queue with a weight reflecting actual priority, say 2 for language-modeling and 1 for multimodal, so that during real contention the higher-priority team gets a proportionally larger share. But weight alone isn't enough -- I'd pair it with a capability cap on each queue, so even during a period when multimodal has no jobs running, language-modeling can't just claim the entire cluster and starve the other team out entirely once they do have work. On top of that, every large job needs to be a gang-scheduled PodGroup with minMember set to its full pod count, because without that, two big jobs can each partially schedule and end up deadlocked, each holding GPUs the other needs to finish forming its own group. And if even the highest-priority job can't get enough capacity, that's a signal for the autoscaler to add nodes -- I wouldn't want the scheduler trying to force a fit that genuinely isn't there.
commonMistakes: Giving both teams equal queues with no weighting, which doesn't reflect actual priority differences
Omitting a capability cap, letting a high-weight queue starve the other team entirely during a one-sided period
Not using gang scheduling via minMember at all, allowing partial scheduling that can deadlock two large jobs
Treating the scheduler as responsible for conjuring capacity that doesn't exist, instead of relying on autoscaling
keyPoints: Queue weight sets relative share during contention; capability caps a queue's absolute maximum to prevent true starvation
Gang scheduling via minMember prevents the specific deadlock case of two large jobs each partially holding GPUs the other needs
Weight and capability solve different problems and are both needed together
A genuine capacity shortfall should trigger autoscaling, not a scheduler workaround

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct weight and capability design
Correctly explains gang-scheduling deadlock prevention
Addresses starvation protection
Mentions autoscaling as the capacity-shortfall response

questions.title: Designing a Model Promotion Pipeline From Challenger to Champion
questions.prompt: Design the stages a newly retrained candidate model must pass through before it's allowed to become the production champion for a fraud-detection model, where a bad promotion has real financial cost. What would you check at each stage, and what's the one-line mechanical act of promotion itself?
questions.modelAnswer: Stage one is an offline comparison against the current champion on a fixed holdout set, checking not just an aggregate metric but segment-level performance, since a model can win in aggregate while losing badly on a specific customer segment. Stage two is a shadow deployment: the candidate receives a mirrored copy of real production traffic, produces real predictions that are logged but never acted on, with zero user-facing risk, which surfaces latency and infrastructure issues the offline comparison can't catch, though it can't tell you about actual business-outcome impact since nothing was acted on. Stage three is a canary: a small, gradually increasing percentage of real traffic actually served by the candidate, with automatic rollback triggers on a hard, sustained metric breach. Only after passing all three does promotion happen, and the promotion itself is a one-line mechanical act, reassigning a registry alias like champion to the candidate's version, deliberately decoupled from any model-weight or infrastructure change so it's instant and trivially reversible.
questions.professionalAnswer: For something with real financial cost riding on it, I wouldn't skip straight from offline metrics to production. Stage one is comparing the candidate against the current champion on a fixed holdout set, and I'd check segment-level performance there, not just the aggregate, since a model can look better overall while quietly getting worse on one specific customer segment. Stage two is shadow deployment -- mirror real traffic to it, log its predictions, never act on them, zero user-facing risk -- which catches latency and infra issues the offline check can't, though it genuinely can't tell me anything about real business-outcome impact since nothing was ever acted on. Stage three is a canary, a small and gradually increasing slice of real traffic, with automatic rollback wired to a hard, sustained metric breach. Only once all three pass does promotion actually happen, and that promotion itself should just be a one-line alias reassignment -- champion pointed at the new version -- deliberately decoupled from any weight or infra change, so it's instant and trivially reversible if something still goes wrong.
commonMistakes: Skipping shadow deployment and going straight from offline comparison to canary
Checking only an aggregate metric in the offline stage, missing segment-level regressions
Not setting up automatic rollback triggers for the canary stage
Conflating the promotion act itself with a model redeploy, rather than a lightweight alias reassignment
keyPoints: Offline comparison should check segment-level performance, not just an aggregate metric
Shadow deployment proves out latency and infra risk with zero user-facing exposure, but can't measure business-outcome impact
A gradually increasing canary is the stage that can measure real business impact at bounded risk
Promotion itself should be a trivial, instantly reversible alias reassignment, decoupled from any weight or infra change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct three-stage design with rationale for each
Correctly identifies shadow deployment's blind spot
Includes an automatic rollback trigger for the canary
Correctly frames promotion as an alias reassignment

questions.title: Designing Multi-Tenant Serving for Many Fine-Tuned Variants of One Base Model
questions.prompt: A product needs to serve roughly 200 customer-specific fine-tuned variants of the same 7B base model, each customer's variant trained via LoRA. Design a serving architecture that doesn't require loading 200 separate full models into GPU memory.
questions.modelAnswer: Load the shared base model's weights once per GPU, and represent each customer's fine-tune as a small LoRA adapter, commonly tens to a few hundred megabytes, applied on top at request time, rather than a full separate model. This is the entire economic case for serving many variants cheaply, since 200 full 7B models would be completely infeasible in GPU memory, while 200 small adapters comfortably coexist alongside one base model. The serving layer needs to resolve which adapter to apply per request by customer ID, keep a cache of recently-used adapters resident and evict cold ones under memory pressure, and batch requests across different adapters together when possible, since the base model's forward pass is shared work even though each request needs its own adapter applied. I'd also plan for the realistic skew in traffic across 200 customers, a small number of highly active customers and a long tail of rarely-used ones, which is exactly the pattern adapter caching and eviction is designed to handle well.
questions.professionalAnswer: The entire reason this is feasible at all is that LoRA lets me load the base model's weights once and treat each customer's fine-tune as a small adapter applied on top, rather than 200 separate full models that would never fit in GPU memory. The serving layer needs a per-request resolution step, figure out which customer's adapter to apply by their ID, plus a caching and eviction policy so recently-used adapters stay resident and cold ones get evicted under memory pressure. I'd also want batching across requests that use different adapters where possible, since the base model's forward pass is shared work regardless of which adapter gets applied on top. And realistically, traffic across 200 customers is going to be skewed, a handful of heavy users and a long tail of rare ones, which is exactly the pattern a good adapter cache is built to handle well, so I'd design the eviction policy around that expected skew rather than assuming uniform usage.
commonMistakes: Loading a full separate model per customer, ignoring LoRA's actual economic point
Not addressing adapter caching and eviction, assuming all 200 can stay resident unconditionally
Ignoring the realistic traffic skew across many tenants when designing the cache eviction policy
Not accounting for batching across requests with different adapters, treating each as needing a fully separate forward pass
keyPoints: LoRA adapters let many fine-tuned variants share one resident base model instead of needing a full model each
A per-request adapter resolution step plus a caching and eviction policy for cold adapters is required at this scale
Traffic skew across many tenants, a few hot users and a long tail of cold ones, should drive the caching policy
Batching across requests with different adapters is possible since the base model's forward pass is shared work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains LoRA's memory economics
Designs adapter resolution plus caching and eviction
Addresses realistic traffic skew
Mentions batching across adapters

questions.title: Protecting an ML Serving Layer From One Slow Downstream Dependency
questions.prompt: Your model-serving layer calls a downstream feature-lookup service on the request path. Design a way to make sure that dependency degrading or failing doesn't take down the whole serving layer's capacity to serve every other request.
questions.modelAnswer: Apply the bulkhead pattern: confine the thread or connection pool used to call the feature-lookup service to its own limited pool, separate from the pool handling everything else, so that dependency filling up its pool when it's slow or down only blocks requests that actually need it, while requests that don't depend on that feature keep flowing through unaffected. Pair that with a circuit breaker on the same dependency: once its recent failure or timeout rate crosses a threshold, stop sending it new requests for a cooldown period rather than letting every request pile up waiting on calls that are likely to fail or time out anyway; during that cooldown, serve a fallback, a cached or default feature value, rather than returning an outright error, if the product can tolerate a degraded-but-not-broken response. Together, the bulkhead limits blast radius and the circuit breaker limits wasted latency on calls unlikely to succeed, two different failure modes of the same dependency, both needing to be handled.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd apply a bulkhead first -- give the feature-lookup service its own isolated connection pool, separate from whatever handles everything else, so when it's slow or down, it can only exhaust its own pool, not drag down requests that don't even need that feature. On top of that I'd add a circuit breaker on the same dependency -- once its failure or timeout rate crosses a threshold, stop sending it new requests for a cooldown instead of letting every request pile up waiting on calls that are probably going to fail anyway. During that cooldown, if the product can tolerate it, I'd serve a fallback -- a cached or default value -- rather than an outright error. I think of these as covering two different failure modes of the same dependency: the bulkhead limits how much damage it can do, and the circuit breaker limits how much time gets wasted on calls that are unlikely to succeed. Neither one alone covers both problems.
commonMistakes: Sharing one connection or thread pool across all downstream calls, letting one slow dependency exhaust resources needed by everything else
Implementing only a circuit breaker without a bulkhead, missing the resource-isolation half of the problem
Returning a hard error during the circuit breaker's open state instead of a fallback, when a fallback was actually acceptable
Not setting a cooldown or half-open retry policy, leaving the breaker permanently open or flapping
keyPoints: A bulkhead isolates the resource pool for one dependency so its failure doesn't exhaust resources needed elsewhere
A circuit breaker stops sending requests to a dependency whose failure rate crosses a threshold, for a cooldown period
The two patterns address different failure modes, resource exhaustion versus wasted latency on doomed calls, and are complementary, not interchangeable
A fallback response during the breaker's open state can keep the product degraded-but-working rather than fully broken

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the bulkhead's resource-isolation purpose
Correctly explains the circuit breaker's threshold/cooldown mechanism
Explains why both are needed together
Mentions fallback behavior

questions.title: Choosing a Storage Tier Strategy for a Large Training Job's Dataset
questions.prompt: A single large training job needs to stream a multi-terabyte dataset to 64 nodes concurrently, with enough throughput that the GPUs are never starved waiting on data. Design the storage tiering for this, explaining why a single storage type isn't the right answer.
questions.modelAnswer: Object storage, such as S3, is the right home for the dataset's durable source of truth, cheap at multi-terabyte scale, and its throughput scales horizontally with more prefixes, but each individual request still carries real latency, typically tens of milliseconds, which is too slow for 512 concurrent GPU-fed data-loading workers hammering it directly at the throughput a training job needs. A parallel filesystem layer, such as FSx for Lustre, sitting in front of S3 with a data-repository association solves this: it lazily loads objects from S3 the first time a job reads them and then serves subsequent reads from its own fast SSD-backed storage, giving the throughput and low per-request latency a parallel filesystem is built for, while S3 stays the durable, cheap long-term store underneath. Block storage attaches to a single instance and simply can't serve as shared storage across 64 nodes at once, so it's not a candidate for the shared dataset at all. And shard count needs to significantly outnumber the total concurrent worker count, roughly 1,000+ shards for 512 concurrent readers here, so no worker ever waits on a shard someone else is still streaming through.
questions.professionalAnswer: A single storage type genuinely doesn't cover this. Object storage is the right place for the dataset's durable copy, cheap at this scale, and its throughput does scale horizontally with more prefixes -- but each individual request still has real latency, tens of milliseconds typically, and 512 concurrent workers hammering it directly just won't hit the throughput a training job like this needs. So I'd put a parallel filesystem in front of it, something like FSx for Lustre with a data-repository association, which lazily pulls objects from S3 on first read and then serves everything after that from its own fast storage. Block storage isn't even in the running here -- it attaches to one instance, it architecturally can't be the shared store across 64 nodes. And I'd make sure shard count significantly outnumbers the worker count, something like 1,000-plus shards for 512 concurrent readers, so nobody's ever stuck waiting on a shard someone else is still streaming through.
commonMistakes: Trying to serve the dataset directly from S3 to all 512 concurrent workers without a caching or parallel-filesystem layer in front
Proposing block storage as shared storage across multiple nodes, which it architecturally cannot do
Not sizing shard count relative to worker count, risking workers stalling on shared shards
Treating local NVMe as viable shared storage rather than per-node scratch space only
keyPoints: Object storage is the right durable, cheap source of truth but has per-request latency too high for direct high-concurrency access
A parallel filesystem with a data-repository association bridges this by lazily caching from object storage onto fast local-equivalent storage
Block storage attaches to one instance and architecturally cannot serve as shared storage across many nodes
Shard count should significantly outnumber concurrent worker count to avoid workers waiting on each other

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct object storage plus parallel filesystem tiering design
Correctly rules out block storage for shared use
Correctly addresses shard-count-versus-worker-count
Gives a coherent justification for why one tier alone fails

questions.title: Designing GPU Sharing for a Shared Research Cluster With Mixed Workload Sizes
questions.prompt: A shared research cluster runs a mix of large full-GPU training jobs and many small experimentation jobs that each only need a fraction of a GPU's memory and compute. Design how you'd let the small jobs share GPUs without starving or corrupting each other, while still letting large jobs claim whole GPUs when they need to.
questions.modelAnswer: For GPUs that support it, A100 or H100-class, partition a subset of the fleet using MIG into several fully isolated instances, each with its own dedicated SMs and memory, which is the right fit for small experimentation jobs specifically because MIG's isolation is real and hardware-level, so one workload on one instance can't be slowed down or crash a workload on a different instance on the same physical card. Time-slicing is a fallback for GPUs that don't support MIG or situations needing more instances than MIG partitioning allows, but it gives no real memory isolation, the GPU scheduler just rotates full-GPU access between workloads in time, so one workload can still exhaust shared memory and slow the others, making it a worse fit for untrusted or noisy small jobs even though it's more flexible in instance count. Large full-GPU training jobs should request whole GPUs from a separate pool of unpartitioned nodes, kept entirely apart from the MIG-partitioned pool, so a big job never has to contend with MIG's fixed instance-size granularity or with time-sliced noisy neighbors.
questions.professionalAnswer: Where the hardware supports it, I'd lean on MIG for the small jobs -- partition a subset of A100 or H100-class GPUs into several isolated instances, each with its own dedicated SMs and memory. That's the right fit specifically because MIG's isolation is real at the hardware level, so one small job can't slow down or crash another one sitting on a different instance of the same physical card. Time-slicing I'd treat as a fallback, not a default -- it gives no real memory isolation at all, it just rotates full-GPU access between workloads in time, so one noisy job can still exhaust shared memory and hurt everyone else sharing that GPU. For the large, full-GPU jobs, I'd keep them in a completely separate, unpartitioned pool, so they never have to contend with MIG's fixed instance sizing or with a time-sliced noisy neighbor -- mixing those pools together just creates scheduling friction nobody needs.
commonMistakes: Using time-slicing as the default sharing mechanism instead of MIG, when MIG's real isolation is available and appropriate
Mixing MIG-partitioned and whole-GPU pools together rather than separating them, causing avoidable scheduling friction
Assuming MIG is available on every GPU generation, including older consumer cards, which it is not
Not accounting for MIG's fixed instance-size granularity as a real constraint on how finely workloads can be split
keyPoints: MIG provides real, hardware-level isolation between instances on the same physical GPU, appropriate for small, mutually-untrusted jobs
Time-slicing provides no memory isolation and should be a fallback, not the default, for sharing GPUs
Large full-GPU jobs should run in a separate, unpartitioned pool rather than contending with MIG instances or time-sliced neighbors
MIG is restricted to specific data-center GPU generations, not universally available

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains MIG's isolation and fit for small jobs
Correctly contrasts time-slicing's lack of isolation
Proposes separate pools for large versus small workloads
Notes MIG's hardware availability constraint

questions.title: Choosing a Serving Stack for a Latency-Sensitive, Single-GPU-Class Product
questions.prompt: You need to serve an 8B-parameter instruction-tuned model for an internal support-chat product, targeting a tight p99 TTFT SLO on a single mid-range GPU, with the team wanting to move fast and not maintain a lot of custom infrastructure. Walk through which serving stack you'd choose among vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and Triton, and why.
questions.modelAnswer: vLLM is the strongest fit here: it's purpose-built for LLM serving specifically, pairing continuous batching with PagedAttention-based KV cache memory management, and it ships as a close-to-production-ready server out of the box, an OpenAI-compatible API, streaming, metrics, without requiring a separate compilation pipeline, matching the team's stated preference to move fast without maintaining a lot of custom infrastructure. TensorRT-LLM would likely squeeze out somewhat better raw throughput and latency by compiling the model into an optimized, GPU-specific executable, but that comes at the cost of a real compilation and engine-maintenance burden, rebuilding engines per model, GPU, and precision combination, that doesn't fit a team wanting to avoid heavy custom infra, and the marginal latency gain may not even matter if the real bottleneck under load turns out to be queuing rather than raw decode speed. Triton is a general-purpose, framework-agnostic server that could host either vLLM or a TensorRT-LLM engine behind one protocol, which is the right layer to add later if this team ends up needing to serve many different model types or backends behind a unified interface, but it's not a reason to choose it over vLLM for a single-model deployment today.
questions.professionalAnswer: Given this team's actual constraints, I'd go with vLLM. It's built specifically for LLM serving, continuous batching plus PagedAttention for KV cache management, and it ships close to production-ready out of the box, an OpenAI-compatible API, streaming, metrics, no separate compilation step to maintain, which fits a team that explicitly wants to move fast without taking on heavy custom infra. TensorRT-LLM would probably squeeze out a bit more raw speed by compiling the model into a GPU-specific executable, but that comes with a real ongoing cost -- rebuilding engines whenever the model, GPU, or precision changes -- and honestly, if the real bottleneck under load turns out to be queuing rather than raw decode speed, that extra compiled speed might not even move the needle on the metric they actually care about. Triton I'd hold off on entirely for now -- it's a backend-agnostic hosting layer, genuinely useful once you're serving several different model types behind one protocol, but there's no reason to add that complexity for a single-model deployment today.
commonMistakes: Choosing TensorRT-LLM by default for 'maximum speed' without weighing the compilation and maintenance cost against the team's actual constraints
Treating Triton as a competitor to vLLM or TensorRT-LLM rather than a layer that can host either
Not checking whether the target GPU and precision are actually well-supported by the chosen stack before committing
Assuming TensorRT-LLM's raw speed advantage would actually move the needle if the real bottleneck is queuing, not decode speed
keyPoints: vLLM fits a team wanting to move fast with a production-ready server and no separate compilation step
TensorRT-LLM trades a real compilation and maintenance burden for better raw execution speed, which may not be worth it for this team's constraints
Triton is a backend-agnostic hosting layer, relevant for multi-model or multi-backend needs, not a reason to pick over vLLM here
The decision should weigh team operational capacity, not just theoretical peak performance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends vLLM with sound reasoning tied to stated constraints
Correctly characterizes TensorRT-LLM's tradeoff
Correctly positions Triton's actual role
Ties the recommendation back to the team's stated priorities

questions.title: Designing SLOs and Alerting for an Inference Service's Latency Commitment
questions.prompt: Design the SLI, SLO, and alerting policy for an inference service that has promised internal stakeholders '99.9% of requests get a response within 2 seconds.' What exactly would you measure, what would the internal target actually be, and how would you decide what pages someone immediately versus what just opens a ticket?
questions.modelAnswer: The SLI is the directly measured value: the percentage of requests completing within 2 seconds, effectively a tail-latency threshold check, measured continuously over a rolling window like 5 minutes for real-time tracking and 28 days for the SLO itself. The SLO should actually be set tighter than the external 99.9% promise, say 99.95% internally, specifically to leave an error-budget margin before the external commitment is actually at risk, since the externally stated number is the floor, not the target to aim exactly at. The error budget is then the allowed share of requests that can miss that internal target before reliability work has to take priority over feature work, for example 0.05% of requests over 28 days. For alerting, I'd split by burn rate: a fast-burn condition, where the budget would be exhausted within hours at the current rate, pages immediately, while a slow-burn condition, exhausted over days, opens a ticket instead of paging, since these represent genuinely different urgency, and alerting on raw metric wobble instead of sustained burn rate would page constantly on momentary blips that don't actually threaten the SLO.
questions.professionalAnswer: The SLI is simple: percentage of requests completing within 2 seconds, measured continuously, maybe a 5-minute window for real-time tracking and 28 days for the SLO itself. But I wouldn't set the internal SLO at exactly 99.9% -- I'd set it tighter, something like 99.95%, specifically to leave myself error-budget margin before the external promise is actually at risk. The external number is the floor, not the target I'm aiming directly at. The error budget then is just the allowed share of misses against that tighter internal target before reliability work has to jump ahead of feature work. For alerting, I'd split by burn rate rather than raw SLI value -- a fast-burn condition, where the budget would be gone in hours at the current rate, pages immediately, while a slow-burn condition that would take days to exhaust just opens a ticket. Those really are different urgencies, and alerting on raw metric wobble instead would just page constantly on blips that don't actually threaten the SLO.
commonMistakes: Setting the internal SLO identical to the external SLA, leaving no margin for error-budget consumption before breaching the external promise
Alerting directly on the SLI value rather than on sustained burn rate, causing alert fatigue from noise
Giving fast-burn and slow-burn conditions the same severity and response path
Not defining the measurement window explicitly, leaving 'percentage of requests' ambiguous over what period
keyPoints: The SLI is the raw measured value; the SLO is the internal target, deliberately set tighter than any external SLA to leave error-budget margin
An error budget quantifies the allowed share of SLO misses before reliability work takes priority over features
Burn-rate-based alerting, not raw SLI thresholds, should drive paging decisions
Fast-burn and slow-burn conditions warrant genuinely different response paths, page versus ticket

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes SLI, SLO, and SLA with correct tightening direction
Correctly defines the error budget
Gives a correct burn-rate-based alerting design
Specifies the measurement windows

questions.title: Pushing Back on an Urgent, Queue-Skipping GPU Request
questions.prompt: A senior ML researcher asks you to manually bump their job to the front of the training queue, bypassing the scheduler, because their deadline is 'tomorrow.' Walk me through how you'd actually handle this conversation and the request.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by taking the urgency seriously rather than dismissing it, and ask specifically what's driving the deadline and what happens if it slips, since that context changes what a reasonable response looks like. Then I'd explain, concretely, why a manual queue-skip is risky beyond just being against policy -- it can deadlock other gang-scheduled jobs, it sets a precedent other researchers will reasonably expect too, and it bypasses whatever fairness mechanism, queue weights, capability caps, exists for a reason. I'd look for a legitimate path that gets them what they actually need without breaking the system for everyone else: checking if their own team's queue has unused capacity or weight headroom, checking if a smaller or cheaper version of their job could start sooner and still hit the deadline, or, if the need is genuinely exceptional, escalating through whatever process exists for a priority exception rather than quietly doing it myself.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct isn't to just say no -- it's to actually understand what's driving the ask. I'd ask what the deadline is really tied to, because sometimes there's a real, legitimate case for an exception, and sometimes it's more that waiting feels uncomfortable. Either way, I'd explain concretely what a manual queue-skip actually risks -- not just 'it's against policy' but that it can starve or even deadlock other teams' gang-scheduled jobs, and that doing it quietly, once, sets an expectation that I'll do it again for the next person with a deadline. Then I'd try to actually solve their problem the right way -- checking if their team has queue headroom they're not using, whether a scoped-down version of the job could realistically hit the deadline, or escalating through whatever real exception process exists instead of making a unilateral call myself. I've found researchers respond a lot better to 'here's why I can't just do that, and here's what I can actually do to help' than to a flat no.
commonMistakes: Giving a flat 'no, that's against policy' without engaging with the underlying need
Quietly granting the exception to avoid conflict, setting a bad precedent
Not explaining the concrete technical risk, starvation or deadlock, behind the policy
Not offering any alternative path that could actually help
keyPoints: Understand the real need behind the urgency before responding
Explain the concrete technical risk, not just 'it's against policy'
Avoid both a flat refusal and a quiet unilateral exception
Offer a legitimate alternative path, such as headroom, a scoped job, or a formal exception process

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Genuinely engages with the underlying need
Explains the concrete risk beyond policy
Avoids both a flat refusal and a unilateral exception
Offers a constructive alternative

questions.title: Handling a 2am Training-Job Failure Under Pressure
questions.prompt: You're paged at 2am because a multi-day training run just failed with no clear error in the logs, and the team is counting on results by morning. Walk me through how you'd actually work the problem, not just what tools you'd use.
questions.modelAnswer: First, I'd resist the urge to immediately start randomly restarting things out of pressure to do something, since that can destroy diagnostic evidence before I've actually looked at it. I'd check the obvious, cheap things first: the last checkpoint's timestamp and whether it's usable, the actual error or warning in the logs, even an unclear failure usually has some signal if you look past the final traceback, and whether this looks like a known failure mode, a hung collective, an Xid error, a straggler, versus something genuinely novel. If I can get the job restarted from the last good checkpoint quickly while the deeper investigation continues in parallel, I'd do that, since restoring progress and understanding root cause aren't mutually exclusive, but I wouldn't report fixed to the team until I actually understand why it failed, because a restart that papers over an unresolved root cause just fails again later, often at a worse time. I'd also communicate proactively rather than going quiet for hours.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I actively fight at 2am is the instinct to just start doing things to feel like I'm making progress. First move is always the cheap, boring checks -- is there a usable checkpoint, what's actually in the logs beyond the top-line error, does this smell like something I've seen before. If I can get the job restarted from the last good checkpoint without losing more progress, I'll do that in parallel with digging into the actual cause, since those two things don't have to be sequential. But I won't tell the team it's fixed until I actually know why it broke -- I've seen a quick restart mask a real problem that just comes back worse a day later. And I try to send a short update even before I have the full picture, because going quiet for three hours while people are waiting is its own kind of failure, even if I'm working the whole time.
commonMistakes: Randomly restarting or changing things immediately out of pressure, destroying diagnostic evidence
Declaring the issue 'fixed' after a restart without actually understanding root cause
Going silent for hours instead of giving interim status updates
Not checking the cheapest, most obvious causes first before escalating to deeper investigation
keyPoints: Resist acting impulsively under pressure; check cheap, obvious causes before deep investigation
A restart from checkpoint and root-cause investigation can proceed in parallel, not sequentially
Don't declare resolution until the actual cause is understood, not just worked around
Proactive, honest status updates matter even without a complete answer yet

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids impulsive action under pressure
Describes a sound diagnostic approach
Distinguishes a restart from true resolution
Mentions proactive communication

questions.title: Explaining a Capacity Tradeoff to a Non-Technical Stakeholder
questions.prompt: A product manager asks why the team can't just 'add more GPUs' to make the new feature's inference latency faster right now, without understanding the cost or timeline implications. How would you actually explain the real tradeoff to them?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd avoid jumping straight into technical jargon and instead frame it in terms they already care about: cost, time, and what actually moves the number they're asking about. I'd explain that adding GPUs mostly helps with how many requests we can handle at once, not necessarily how fast any single request comes back -- if the current latency problem is actually about a single request being slow, more GPUs wouldn't fix that at all, it would just let more slow requests happen in parallel. Then I'd lay out the real options with their actual tradeoffs in plain terms: more GPUs, cost scales roughly linearly, helps with volume not necessarily per-request speed, can often be done this week; a smaller or faster model, helps the actual latency number but needs engineering time and might cost some quality; or inference-level optimizations the team's already planning, helps latency with no quality cost, but takes longer to build. I'd be honest that I don't have a magic lever that gets them everything, fast, cheap, and immediate, and let them make an informed call.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start with jargon -- I'd start with what they actually care about, which is usually the number, the cost, and the timeline. First thing I'd clarify is that more GPUs mostly buys us more volume, how many requests we can handle at once, not necessarily a faster single response. If the actual complaint is that one request feels slow, more GPUs just means more slow requests running in parallel, it doesn't touch the thing they're actually unhappy about. Then I'd lay out the real options honestly: more GPUs is fast to do and scales cost roughly linearly, but might not move their number at all; a smaller or faster model would actually help latency, but needs engineering time and might cost some quality; inference optimizations we're already planning would help with no quality tradeoff but take longer. I don't have a lever that's fast, cheap, and solves everything at once, and I'd rather tell them that plainly than let them think adding GPUs is a magic fix.
commonMistakes: Launching into technical jargon, KV cache, batching, quantization, without translating it to the stakeholder's actual concerns
Not distinguishing between a throughput problem and a per-request latency problem when explaining why 'more GPUs' might not help
Presenting only one option instead of laying out the real tradeoff space
Overpromising a fix that doesn't actually address the stakeholder's real bottleneck
keyPoints: Translate the technical tradeoff into terms the stakeholder actually cares about, cost, timeline, the specific number they want
Distinguish throughput, where more GPUs helps, from per-request latency, where more GPUs may not help, explicitly
Lay out multiple real options with honest tradeoffs rather than one answer
Be honest about what can and can't be achieved rather than overpromising

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Translates the technical reality into stakeholder-relevant terms
Correctly distinguishes throughput from latency
Presents multiple honest options
Avoids overpromising

questions.title: Disagreeing With a Teammate Over Kubeflow vs. Slurm
questions.prompt: You and a teammate disagree about whether the team's next training cluster should be orchestrated with Kubeflow/Kubernetes or Slurm. You lean one way, they lean the other, and it's becoming a bit of a standoff. How do you actually work through this?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd first make sure the disagreement is actually about the technical tradeoff and not just two people anchored on what they're each more comfortable with, and I'd ask what specifically they think the other option gets us that the one I prefer doesn't, in terms of our actual workload, not in the abstract. I'd lay out the real tradeoffs honestly on both sides: Slurm has decades of HPC-world maturity for exactly this kind of large, homogeneous multi-node training job and a simpler operational model for a team not already running Kubernetes for anything else, while Kubernetes/Kubeflow gives one platform for both training and serving, better integration with already-Kubernetes infrastructure, and a larger hiring pool. If we can't converge through discussion alone, I'd propose a cheap way to get real evidence instead of continuing to argue from priors, a small pilot of each on a representative job, measuring actual setup time and operational pain, and commit in advance to abiding by what that pilot actually shows, even if it goes against my own initial lean.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd check is whether this is actually a technical disagreement or just two people anchored on what they're each more comfortable with -- I'd ask specifically what they think the other option gets us on our actual workload, not in the abstract. Then I'd lay out both sides honestly, including the case against my own preference: Slurm's got decades of maturity for exactly this kind of large, homogeneous training job and a simpler operational model if we're not already running Kubernetes for anything else; Kubernetes gives us one platform across training and serving and plugs into infrastructure we already run. If we're still stuck after that, I'd rather run a small, cheap pilot of both on a real job and measure actual setup time and pain than keep arguing from priors -- and I'd commit up front to going with whatever the pilot actually shows, even if it goes against what I originally leaned toward.
commonMistakes: Treating the disagreement as a battle to win rather than a decision to get right
Arguing from personal preference or familiarity without being explicit that that's part of the disagreement
Not proposing any way to get actual evidence, letting the disagreement stay purely theoretical
Refusing to commit to the pilot's outcome in advance, making the exercise pointless
keyPoints: Separate genuine technical tradeoff disagreement from personal comfort or familiarity bias
Lay out both sides' real tradeoffs honestly, not just defending your own position
Propose a concrete, cheap way to gather real evidence, such as a small pilot, rather than arguing from priors indefinitely
Commit in advance to respecting what the evidence shows, even against your own initial lean

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies and separates preference from genuine tradeoff
Fairly represents both sides' real tradeoffs
Proposes a concrete evidence-gathering approach
Shows willingness to be wrong

questions.title: Prioritizing Platform Reliability Work Against a Backlog of Feature Requests
questions.prompt: Your platform team has a backlog full of feature requests from model teams, but you believe a chunk of reliability work, better alerting, checkpoint retention cleanup, a flaky scheduler bug, needs to happen first. How do you actually make that case and get it prioritized?
questions.modelAnswer: I wouldn't just assert reliability first as a principle, I'd make the case concretely, in terms of actual cost: how many engineer-hours has the flaky scheduler bug already burned in lost training time and manual intervention, how close is unmanaged checkpoint storage growth to actually becoming an incident rather than a slow background cost, and what's the realistic blast radius if the missing alerting means a real outage goes undetected for hours instead of minutes. I'd frame this against the feature requests using the same currency, not reliability matters more as a value, but here's the quantified cost of not doing this, compared to the quantified value of the next features in line, so the prioritization conversation is apples to apples rather than a philosophical argument. Where I can, I'd also look for a middle path: can a critical piece of reliability work be scoped small enough to land alongside a highest-priority feature rather than as a full stop on the backlog.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't lead with 'reliability should come first' as a value statement, because that's not actually a persuasive argument on its own. I'd quantify it instead -- how many engineer-hours has the flaky scheduler bug already cost us in lost training time and manual firefighting, how close is the checkpoint storage growth to becoming an actual incident rather than just a slow background cost, what's the real blast radius if the missing alerting means an outage goes undetected for hours instead of minutes. Then I'd frame that against the feature backlog in the same currency the stakeholders already use to value those features, so it's an apples-to-apples comparison, not a philosophical argument about values. And where I can, I'd look for a middle path -- scoping the most critical piece of reliability work small enough that it can land alongside the top feature priority, rather than presenting it as a full stop on everything else.
commonMistakes: Asserting reliability should come first as a value statement without quantifying the actual cost of not doing it
Treating this as an all-or-nothing choice rather than looking for a way to interleave both
Not translating the reliability work's cost into the same terms stakeholders use to value features
Letting the backlog sit unaddressed indefinitely rather than scoping a minimal reliability fix that unblocks the bigger work
keyPoints: Quantify the real cost of the reliability gap, lost engineer-hours and growing risk, rather than asserting a value judgment
Frame the comparison in the same terms stakeholders use for feature value, not a separate argument
Look for a middle path that interleaves scoped reliability work with top feature priorities
Avoid treating prioritization as all-or-nothing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Quantifies the real cost rather than asserting a principle
Frames the comparison in stakeholder-relevant terms
Proposes a practical middle path
Avoids all-or-nothing framing

questions.title: Owning a Mistake That Caused a Production Incident
questions.prompt: You pushed a config change that you believed was safe, and it caused a brief but real outage in the inference service. Walk me through how you'd actually handle this, from the moment you realize it was your change.
questions.modelAnswer: The first move is acting fast and transparently, not protecting myself -- I'd immediately say in the incident channel that I believe my change caused this, roughly when it went out, and what I'm doing to mitigate it, usually a rollback, rather than staying quiet while others investigate something I already have a strong hunch about. Once the immediate impact is mitigated, I'd write an honest postmortem that actually explains what I missed in my own reasoning, not a vague 'a config change caused an issue' but specifically what I believed would be safe and why that belief was wrong, since the useful part of a postmortem for everyone else is understanding the actual gap in my own mental model, not just the mechanical sequence of events. I'd also look for what would have caught this before production, a missing staging or canary step, a validation check that should have existed, and treat the real fix as closing that gap, not just 'I'll be more careful next time.'
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I suspect it's my change, I'd say so in the incident channel right away -- roughly when it went out, what I believe caused it, and what I'm doing about it, usually rolling it back. I wouldn't sit quietly while other people investigate something I already have a strong hunch about just to avoid the awkwardness of being wrong in public. Once the immediate impact is handled, I'd write a postmortem that's actually specific about what I got wrong in my own reasoning -- not 'a config change caused an outage' but exactly what I believed was safe and why that belief turned out to be incorrect, because that's the part that's actually useful for anyone reading it later. And I'd push myself to find a real process fix -- a missing canary step, a validation check that should have caught this -- rather than letting 'I'll be more careful' stand in as the resolution, because that's not something anyone can actually rely on.
commonMistakes: Staying quiet or hedging about being the cause while others investigate, delaying mitigation
Writing a vague postmortem that doesn't explain the actual gap in reasoning that led to the mistake
Treating 'I'll be more careful' as sufficient instead of identifying a real process or tooling fix
Being defensive rather than straightforwardly owning the mistake
keyPoints: Speak up immediately and specifically once you suspect your own change caused the issue, rather than staying quiet
Mitigate first, usually a rollback, and investigate root cause in parallel or after
A good postmortem explains the actual gap in reasoning, not just the mechanical sequence of events
The real fix is a process or tooling change that would catch this class of mistake, not a personal resolution to be more careful

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Immediate, transparent ownership
Correct mitigate-first sequencing
Honest, specific postmortem reasoning
Identifies a real systemic fix

questions.title: Getting a Skeptical Team to Adopt a New Paved-Road Platform Tool
questions.prompt: You've built a shared feature store that would save a model team real time, but they're skeptical and comfortable with their current ad hoc pipeline. How do you actually get them to adopt it, without just mandating it from above?
questions.modelAnswer: I wouldn't lead with 'this is the new standard, please migrate', I'd start by understanding what's actually working for them about their current ad hoc setup, since skepticism toward a platform tool is usually rooted in a real, specific pain point from a past tool that didn't deliver. I'd look for the smallest, lowest-risk way to demonstrate real value on their own problem, migrating one feature, or one new model, rather than asking for a full migration up front, so they can see the actual benefit, less duplicated logic, no training/serving skew risk, on something real rather than taking my word for it on a hypothetical. I'd also be honest about the tool's actual limitations rather than overselling it, since nothing kills adoption trust faster than a platform team that oversold something and then the gaps show up in production. If after a real trial they're still not convinced, I'd want to understand specifically why, since that feedback might mean the tool genuinely isn't ready for their use case yet.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't open with 'this is the new standard, please migrate' -- that tends to produce compliance, not actual buy-in. I'd start by understanding what's specifically behind their skepticism, because it's usually rooted in a real, past experience with some other tool that didn't deliver, not pure resistance to change. Then I'd look for the smallest possible way to show real value on something they actually have, migrating one feature or one new model, rather than asking for a full migration commitment before they've seen any payoff. I'd also be upfront about what the tool doesn't do well yet, because overselling it and having the gaps surface later in production is exactly what destroys trust in a platform team going forward. Asking for a full migration commitment before any small-scale proof of value

Demonstrate value on a small, real, low-risk slice before asking for full adoption
Be honest about the tool's actual limitations instead of overselling it

questions.title: Telling a Peer Their Deployment Practice Is Risky
questions.prompt: A peer on another team has started directly editing production Kubernetes resources with kubectl edit during incidents instead of going through the normal deploy pipeline, and it's worked out fine so far. How would you actually raise this with them?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd raise it privately and specifically, not as a general lecture about best practices, and I'd frame it around the actual risk rather than the fact that it broke a rule: a manual kubectl edit during an incident isn't tracked anywhere, so the next person investigating a weird production state has no record of what changed or why, and the next regular deploy through the pipeline can silently overwrite that manual edit, undoing a fix nobody remembers making. I'd acknowledge genuinely that it's worked out fine so far, that's real, not dismissible, but 'worked out so far' isn't the same as 'safe', and I'd rather have this conversation now, calmly, than after it causes a real problem during a worse incident. I'd also try to solve the actual underlying need: if the normal deploy pipeline is too slow for genuine incident response, that's a real gap worth fixing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd bring this up privately, one on one, not as a general lecture, and I'd frame it around the actual risk rather than 'you broke a rule.' A manual kubectl edit during an incident leaves no record anywhere, so the next person investigating a strange production state has nothing to go on, and worse, the next normal deploy through the pipeline can silently overwrite that fix without anyone remembering it was ever there. questions.title: Balancing Speed and Safety When a Research Team Wants to Skip Review
questions.prompt: A research team under deadline pressure asks to push a training config change directly to the shared cluster without going through the usual review, 'just this once.' How do you handle this?

If the change is genuinely low-risk, scoped to their own resources, no shared-state impact, I'd look for a fast-path review, a 10-minute async check from someone, rather than either a flat no or skipping review entirely, since 'just this once' quietly becoming 'we don't really do review under pressure' is a real risk for a shared platform. questions.professionalAnswer: I'd want to understand what this specific review step actually catches before deciding anything, because not all review is equally risky to skip -- catching a style issue is very different from catching a resource request that could starve someone else's job. questions.title: A Design Decision That Didn't Pan Out

questions.title: Navigating Two Teams With Conflicting Priorities on the Same Cluster

questions.title: Explaining Why You Declined a Reasonable-Sounding Data Request
questions.prompt: A product team asks you to add a seemingly simple feature to a training pipeline: joining in a new customer-behavior dataset that would improve model quality, but you know it includes data the model shouldn't be trained on for a data-retention or compliance reason they don't realize. How do you handle saying no?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd explain the specific constraint clearly rather than just refusing, since the product team almost certainly isn't aware of the retention or compliance boundary and would want to know it exists, a flat no with no explanation reads as arbitrary and erodes trust, while 'here's specifically what this dataset includes and why it's out of bounds' gives them the information to actually understand and plan around it. I'd be concrete about the actual boundary, which fields or records are restricted, and why, rather than a vague 'compliance says no', since specificity is what lets them figure out whether there's a narrower, compliant version of what they actually need. I'd also actively help find an alternative that gets closer to their real goal within the actual constraint, maybe an aggregated or anonymized version of the same signal is compliant even though the raw data isn't, rather than leaving them with nothing once the door closes on their original ask.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say no -- that reads as arbitrary to a team that genuinely doesn't know the constraint exists, and it burns trust for no good reason. I'd explain specifically what's actually restricted and why, which fields or records, not just a vague 'compliance says no,' because that specificity is what actually lets them figure out if there's a narrower version of what they need that is compliant. And I wouldn't stop at explaining the boundary -- I'd actively try to find an alternative that still gets them closer to their real goal, maybe an aggregated or anonymized version of the same signal works fine even though the raw data doesn't. I think of this as both a compliance boundary and a product problem worth solving together, not just a gate I'm closing on them.
